metaTitle: Lost Share Certificate & RJSC Transfer in Bangladesh
title: Lost Share Certificate & RJSC Transfer in Bangladesh
metaDescription: Replace a lost physical share certificate and complete RJSC Form 117 share transfers in Bangladesh under the Companies Act 1994 with indemnity steps.
heroIntro: Under Section 38 and Schedule I (Table A, Regulation 8) of the Companies Act, 1994, a shareholder or NRB director in Bangladesh who loses a physical share certificate can obtain a duplicate certificate by filing a police General Diary (GD), publishing a newspaper notice, executing an Indemnity Bond on non-judicial stamp paper, and passing a Board Resolution before filing Form 117 at RJSC.

sections.h2: Legal Basis Under the Companies Act, 1994
sections.content:
Section 84 of the Companies Act, 1994 makes a share certificate under the common seal of the company prima facie evidence of a member's title to those shares. Where a certificate is defaced, lost, or destroyed, Schedule I, Table A, Regulation 8 (and corresponding Articles of Association) authorises the Board of Directors to issue a duplicate share certificate upon satisfactory proof of loss and an indemnity against third-party claims.

Under Section 38 of the Companies Act, 1994, a company cannot register a transfer of shares unless a proper instrument of transfer (Form 117) executed by both transferor and transferee is delivered along with the share certificate. Consequently, NRB investors or family members seeking to sell or inherit company shares cannot complete an RJSC transfer until the missing certificate is lawfully replaced.

For wider corporate governance obligations, see our guides on company annual compliance in Bangladesh and company director liability.

sections.h2: When Duplicate Share Certificates Are Required at RJSC
sections.content:
A formal duplicate-issuance process is mandatory whenever original share scrips are missing prior to a share sale, bank loan pledge, succession transmission, or RJSC audit. Simply reprinting a certificate without a Board Resolution and Indemnity Bond exposes directors to personal liability under Section 43 of the Companies Act, 1994 if the original certificate later surfaces in the hands of a bona fide pledgee.

In family-owned private limited companies, disputes often arise when one shareholder refuses to hand over physical share certificates or claims they were lost during office relocation. If minority shareholders face obstruction during share transmission or board exclusion, remedies exist under Section 233 minority shareholder protection, or you can consult a corporate lawyer in Bangladesh.

sections.h2: Step-by-Step Procedure to Issue a Duplicate Share Certificate
sections.content:
Companies registered with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RJSC) should follow a strict six-step sequence to make the duplicate certificate legally defensible.

  1. File a Police General Diary (GD): Lodge a GD at the local police station (or through an authorised representative for NRBs) recording the share certificate number, folio number, and distinctive share numbers.
  2. Publish a Public Newspaper Notice: Issue a notice in at least one widely circulated Bangla and English daily newspaper giving 7 to 14 days for any claimant to object.
  3. Execute an Indemnity Bond: The shareholder signs a notarised Indemnity Bond on non-judicial stamp paper (governed by the Stamp Act, 1899) indemnifying the company against loss from the missing original.
  4. Convene a Board Meeting: The Board of Directors reviews the GD, newspaper clipping, and Indemnity Bond, and passes a formal resolution approving cancellation of the old scrip and issuance of a duplicate marked 'DUPLICATE'.
  5. Update the Register of Members: Record the duplicate certificate number and cancellation note in the statutory Register of Members under Section 34 of the Companies Act, 1994.
  6. Proceed with RJSC Form 117 & Schedule X: If a share transfer is planned, execute Form 117 with stamp duty paid and reflect the updated shareholding in the next Schedule X Annual Return.

sections.h2: Compliance Comparison: Duplicate Issue vs. Form 117 Transfer
sections.content:
Issuing a duplicate certificate is an internal company-register action backed by Board approval, whereas a share transfer or transmission requires statutory RJSC filing and stamp duty payment.

ActionGoverning ProvisionRJSC Filing Required?Key Legal Requirement
Duplicate Share CertificateTable A, Reg. 8, Companies Act 1994Internal Register (Optional notice)Police GD, Newspaper Notice, Indemnity Bond, Board Resolution.
Share Transfer (Sale/Gift)Section 38, Companies Act 1994Yes (Form 117 + Schedule X)Executed Form 117, Stamp Duty (1.5% on consideration), Certificate.
Transmission on DeathSection 38 Proviso & Succession Act 1925Yes (Schedule X)Succession Certificate / Probate + Board Resolution.

Where a shareholder has passed away, heirs must first obtain a Succession Certificate from the District Judge Court before the Board can transmit shares.

Prepare the following authenticated documents before requesting the company secretary or legal counsel to place the matter before the Board.

  • Written application to the Board of Directors specifying folio number, certificate number, and distinctive share numbers.
  • Copy of the Police General Diary (GD) and original newspaper tear-sheets showing the public loss notice.
  • Notarised Indemnity Bond on non-judicial stamp paper (for NRBs, attested by the Bangladesh Embassy/High Commission and MOFA—see our attestation guide).
  • Certified Board Resolution and updated Register of Members extract signed by the Managing Director/Chairman.
  • Shareholder NID/passport copy, RJSC Memorandum & Articles of Association, and Form 117 (if transferring shares).

If your company faces director deadlock or winding-up risks, review our guide on company winding up in Bangladesh or consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam via our contact page for a free initial consultation.

faqs.question: Can an NRB shareholder apply for a duplicate share certificate without visiting Dhaka?
faqs.answer: Yes. An NRB shareholder can authorise a local representative in Dhaka via an Embassy-attested Power of Attorney to file the police GD, publish the newspaper notice, and submit the notarised Indemnity Bond to the company's Board of Directors.

faqs.question: How much stamp duty applies to a share transfer Form 117 in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Under the Stamp Act, 1899 (as amended), share transfer instruments (Form 117) attract ad valorem stamp duty based on the consideration value of the shares being transferred. Because official stamp rates are updated periodically, verify the current RJSC challan schedule before filing.

faqs.question: What if the company directors refuse to issue a duplicate share certificate?
faqs.answer: If the Board unreasonably refuses to issue a duplicate certificate or rectify the Register of Members after receiving a valid GD and Indemnity Bond, the aggrieved shareholder can petition the High Court Division (Company Bench) under Section 43 or Section 233 of the Companies Act, 1994.

faqs.question: Does a lost share certificate have to be reported to RJSC directly?
faqs.answer: The Companies Act, 1994 places the responsibility for issuing duplicate share certificates and maintaining the Register of Members on the company's Board of Directors. However, if the duplicate certificate is needed to complete a Form 117 transfer or Schedule X filing, RJSC verifies the updated records.

faqs.question: How long should a company wait after publishing a newspaper notice before issuing a duplicate?
faqs.answer: Standard corporate practice in Bangladesh allows 7 to 14 days from the date of publication in a national daily newspaper for any third party claiming a lien or pledge over the lost certificate to submit written objections to the company's registered office.
